methodological_questions: Exogeneity of lineup changes: are substitutions independent of game context?
Measurement of shot mix after lineup change: time window and shot type granularity
Statistical power with large number of possessions but many categories
Causal identification of offensive five effects on shot mix

historical_evidence.finding: Offenses attack the rim more when the opponent has no big on the floor: rim share +0.123 (SE 0.295), 3PA -1.79pp (SE 0.31), PPP +0.008 (SE 0.007). Effects imprecise; small sample warnings.
PULL_UP exposure-effect decline was an artifact of lineup confounding: with lineup FE slope -0.0255, without only -0.0063; placebo on other play types similar, indicating shooter-level confound.
Lineup, process/usage, and context explain nearly zero additional variance in H1→H2 PPP collapse beyond regression to the mean (RTM 32.9%, lineup 0.0%). Adequately powered null for lineup effects.

Within-game defensive adaptation to repeated play type slope -0.0019 PPP/exposure (SE 0.0019); only PULL_UP effect significant after multiplicity correction. Low measurement reliability and insufficient exposure noted.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Attempt to estimate exposure-effect without accounting for lineup confounding
failed_approaches.why: C_artifact: apparent effect vanished without lineup FE; shooter selection confounds the exposure relationship.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Trying to explain PPP collapse via lineup/process/context
failed_approaches.why: B_powered_null: lineup changes added 0.0% explanatory power beyond regression to the mean.
LIM:insufficient_exposure and LIM:low_measurement_reliability led to null except for a single play type.

evidence_establishes: Shot mix can respond to opponent lineup changes (SF34), but the effect is small and measured imprecisely.
Lineup confounding can create spurious effects if not controlled with shooter or lineup fixed effects (SF-TMP-009).
Lineup changes do not explain in-game performance variance well (SF-APPS-076), suggesting that detecting a consistent shot-mix shift after offensive substitutions may be challenging.
Within-game effects tend to be tiny except for isolated play types (SF38), advising against expecting large shifts from a single lineup change.
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether changing the offensive five itself produces a detectable shift in shot mix; no prior study tested this directly.
The magnitude of any offensive-five-induced shot-mix change in a well-controlled design.
That confounding by game situation can be fully eliminated, only that it is a known threat.
own_inferences: The play-by-play and substitution rotation data are sufficient to construct a before-after comparison of shot mix around offensive substitutions.
A naive comparison will be severely confounded because substitutions often correlate with game state (score, period, foul trouble, fatigue), which also influence shot selection.

Historical imprecision (SF34) and the negligible lineup variance (SF-APPS-076) suggest the true effect may be small, requiring a large sample and careful confounding control to avoid a null or spurious result.

Using a regression discontinuity around substitution timestamps, together with team/game-state fixed effects and shooter fixed effects, can mitigate some confounding, but residual endogeneity may remain.
uncertainties: Ideal time window length after a substitution to capture shot-mix change while avoiding overlapping substitutions.
How much defensive lineup changes co-occur with offensive changes and contaminate the estimate.
The actual effect size is unknown; power calculations will need plausible range based on SF34 and SF38.
Whether the design will be considered a valid demonstration of personnel-effect detectability if results are null.

historical_effect.explanation: The historical evidence (SF34's imprecise opponent-lineup effect, SF-TMP-009's lineup-confounding artifact, and SF-APPS-076's null lineup contribution) shifted the decision from a simple before-after test to a design that incorporates shooter fixed effects, placebo falsification, and explicit confounding controls. Without this history, the natural experiment might have been accepted as trivially detectable.

blocking_constraints.text: Substitutions are not random; they co-vary with game context, which independently affects shot selection. Residual confounding may produce spurious or masked effects.

If the true shot-mix shift is as small as the imprecise effects seen in SF34 (rim share +0.123, SE 0.295), even a three-season sample may lack power to detect it, especially after multiplicity correction across shot categories.

prior_work.summary: No prior study tested the exact question of whether an offensive lineup change itself shifts shot mix; SF34 examined opponent lineup changes and found inconclusive results, while SF-TMP-009 illustrated that lineup confounding can produce artifacts.

risks.text: Game situation (score, period, time remaining) drives both substitutions and shot selection; failure to fully account for this may bias estimates.
With many shot-type categories and potential small effects, the study may be underpowered, leading to a false null.
Play-type classification (drive, post-up, etc.) in the derived graph database must be consistent; any noise inflates variance.
A simple before-after comparison without a plausible control group (e.g., pseudo-substitution moments) may mistake natural shot-mix variation for a substitution effect.
Testing many shot-mix proportions simultaneously (3PA%, rim%, midrange%, play-type frequencies) inflates the family-wise error rate if not adjusted.

design.estimand: The causal effect of an offensive lineup change (at least one player substitution) on the subsequent distribution of shot types, compared to the distribution in the immediately preceding possessions within the same game, after controlling for game-state confounders. The primary estimand is the average treatment effect across all such changes, with a secondary examination of heterogeneity by player quality discrepancy.
design.unit: A substitution episode: a stoppage where the offensive five changes, for which we can define a clean pre-window (last 10 offensive possessions before the stoppage) and post-window (first 10 offensive possessions after the stoppage) without overlapping other offensive substitutions. Possession-level outcomes (shot type indicator) are aggregated within episode to proportions.
design.sample: All NBA regular-season and playoff games from 2022-23 through 2024-25 as available, restricted to episodes where: the offensive lineup change occurs during a stoppage (substitution explicitly recorded in play-by-play); at least 5 possessions exist in both pre- and post-window; and the same team remains on offense (no change of possession before the window). Exclude substitutions that occur in the last 2 minutes of a game due to extreme strategic selection.
design.power: Pilot analysis on a held-out season to estimate effect size; given three seasons (~3,900 games, thousands of substitution episodes), minimal detectable effect sizes are ~0.02 in a proportion with 80% power. Historical precedent (SF34 rim share +0.12 with SE 0.29) suggests a true effect >0.05 may be detectable; if effect is smaller, the study may be underpowered.
design.controls: Fixed effects: team-season (interacted), game-quarter bin, score differential (spread <=4 categories), period-quarter interaction. Shooter-level fixed effects (player dummy) to absorb individual shooting tendencies. Control for opponent defensive lineup change occurring simultaneously (binary indicator and interaction). Standard errors clustered at game level.
design.falsification: Placebo test: identify control windows of the same length within the same game when no offensive substitution occurred but game state is matched on score differential, period, and minutes elapsed. Compare shot-mix changes in these placebo windows to the true substitution episodes; a genuine effect should be significantly larger. Additionally, test whether shot mix changes at defensive-only substitutions (when offense stays the same) zero out, serving as a negative exposure.
design.multiplicity: Pre-specify a hierarchical family: (primary) overall shot-type distribution shift using a chi-squared test on rim (<8ft), mid-range, three-point; (secondary) individual play-type shares (drive, post-up, catch-and-shoot etc.) with Holm-Bonferroni correction. All analyses will be pre-registered.
design.decision_rule: Reject the null of no shift if the chi-squared test (or equivalent multinomial regression likelihood-ratio test) yields p < 0.05 after clustering, and the placebo test shows no comparable effect. Effect sizes and confidence intervals will be reported regardless of significance.
design.data_version: NBA stats API play-by-play and substitution rotation records for 2022-23 through 2024-25 seasons, plus the derived play-type possession graph database as of 2026-11-02.

Measurement of shot mix after lineup change: time window and shot type granularity
Statistical power with lineup combination sparsity
Causal identification of offensive five effects on shot mix

system_prompt:
You are a basketball analytics researcher deciding whether and how a research question should be studied.
You work only from the task statement and the tools listed below. Do not assume facts you have not seen.

The work has two stages, in this order.
Stage 1, retrieval:
1. Read the research objective and the data description.
2. Identify the research concepts and methodological questions the task raises.
3. Retrieve historical evidence by calling retrieve_history.
In stage 1 do not assess the question, predict outcomes or decide. Your only stage-1 reply is the retrieve_history call.
Stage 2, assessment, after the retrieval result is returned:
4. Summarise the relevant historical findings and failed approaches.
5. State what the historical evidence does and does not establish.
6. Assess whether the research question is testable.
7. Identify methodological risks and potential confounders.
8. Make the final research decision.
9. Explain whether and how the historical evidence changed the decision.
The stage-2 output format is given together with the retrieval result.

Evidence rules: keep what a retrieved record states (historical_evidence and failed_approaches, each citing the
identifier of a returned record and its status exactly as recorded) separate from your own inference and from
uncertainty or missing information. Cite only identifiers returned by a tool, and never describe an earlier study that
no tool returned. In some settings retrieval returns no records; then state that no historical evidence was available.

Tools:
- retrieve_history(research_concepts, methodological_questions, query): the prescribed retrieval step. Returns the most relevant consolidated study-family records of earlier research by this project that are available in this setting, with their identifiers; returns an empty list when none are available.
- glossary(): definitions of basketball and project terms used in task statements.
- data_catalog(): the fields available in each per-game data file.
- search_documents(query): rank further study-family documents by text relevance; returns up to 4 families not yet returned.
- read_family(id): the complete record of one study family (for example 'FAM:SF-APPA-001').

Protocol: every reply is exactly one JSON object and nothing else.
To call a tool: {"action": "tool", "tool": "<name>", "args": {...}}
To finish (stage 2 only): {"action": "final", "output": <object following the stage-2 schema>}
You may call at most 12 tools; then you must finish. Check that every opening brace has a closing brace.

Risk codes (use only these): SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER, EXPOSURE_SPARSITY, MEASURE_RELIABILITY, RTM_SELECTION, OUTCOME_DERIVED_LABEL, LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD, MECHANICAL_FLOOR, BASE_RATE, CONFOUNDING, LABEL_ERROR, PLACEBO_DEPENDENCE, MULTIPLE_TESTING, IMPLEMENTATION_BUG, DRIFT_NONSTATIONARITY

Research question (as posed on 2026-11-02, in the area of lineup and matchup effects):
Changing the offensive five itself moves shot mix, showing the design can detect personnel effects.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

Stage 1. Reply only with the retrieval call: {"action": "tool", "tool": "retrieve_history", "args": {"research_concepts": ["..."], "methodological_questions": ["..."], "query": "..."}}

We are in Stage 1, so we need to identify the research concepts and methodological questions, then call retrieve_history with them.

Research question: "Changing the offensive five itself moves shot mix, showing the design can detect personnel effects."

Interpretation: The researcher wants to test whether changing the offensive five (i.e., lineup substitutions, altering the set of offensive players on the court) causes changes in shot mix (the distribution of shot types, such as shot distance, shot type like catch-and-shoot vs. pull-up, play type, etc.). The claim is that this "shows the design can detect personnel effects" – possibly a methodological demonstration that the experimental or observational design (e.g., using lineup changes as a natural experiment) can detect effects of player personnel on shot selection.

So the research concepts are about lineup changes, offensive five, shot mix, personnel effects. Methodological questions likely involve causal identification from lineup changes (e.g., do substitutions provide exogenous variation?), measurement of shot mix, potential confounders (e.g., defense, game situation), and sparsity of lineup combinations.

Let's identify concepts:
- Offensive lineup changes / substitutions
- Shot mix (distribution of shot types)
- Personnel effects on shot selection
- Natural experiment / design to detect effects

Methodological questions:
- Can lineup changes be treated as exogenous shocks to the offensive five? (Confounding by game context, score, opponent, coaching decisions)
- What is the appropriate time window to measure shot mix after a change? (Immediate possessions following a substitution)
- How to measure shot mix reliably? (Sample size per lineup, granularity of shot types)
- How to isolate offensive changes from simultaneous defensive changes? (Defensive matchups also change with substitutions)
- Are there enough lineup variation and possessions to have statistical power?

We'll also provide a query string that encapsulates the research question. Now, call retrieve_history with those.

We need to complete steps 4-9. The retrieval returned 4 records: FAM:SF34, FAM:SF-TMP-009, FAM:SF-APPS-076, FAM:SF38. They are all somewhat related to lineup/personnel effects on shot mix or offensive behavior, but none directly test the exact question: "Changing the offensive five itself moves shot mix, showing the design can detect personnel effects." The question seems to be about whether a natural experiment where you change the offensive lineup (substitutions) results in a detectable shift in shot mix (distribution of shot types). The research concept: offensive lineup changes themselves cause shot mix changes, perhaps as a way to validate a design that isolates personnel effects. The goal might be to show that simply changing the lineup alters shot distribution, suggesting the design can detect such effects. But we need to interpret the task: "Changing the offensive five itself moves shot mix, showing the design can detect personnel effects." That sounds like a methodological demonstration: if we take instances where the offense subs out one or more players, does the shot mix change? If yes, it demonstrates that the design (perhaps using within-game variation) has enough signal to detect personnel-induced changes in shot selection. So the question is testable if we have data on substitutions, shot types, and enough variation.

The records include:

- FAM:SF34: opponent lineup adaptation: shot mix when opposing rim big is off floor. That is about the defense's lineup (no big) affecting offensive shot mix. It found weak effects on rim share (Rim share +0.123 with SE 0.295), inconclusive. So that is about DEFENSIVE lineup changes, not offensive five changes. Still somewhat relevant: shows that shot mix can change with lineup variation, but the effect was noisy.

- FAM:SF-TMP-009: PULL_UP exposure-effect diagnostics. That is about within-game exposure to pull-up shots and effectiveness, found artifact due to lineup confounding. That indicates that lineup changes can confound exposure effects, relevant. It also shows that lineup fixed effects were essential. So when analyzing shot mix changes after a lineup change, need to control for shooter fixed effects, maybe.

- FAM:SF-APPS-076: Trigger attribution of half-to-half PPP collapse. They looked at lineup changes as part of explaining suppression triggers, and found lineup added 0.0% to variance. That suggests that lineup changes did not explain the phenomenon, but it's about a different metric (PPP collapse). Not directly relevant.

- FAM:SF38: Defensive in-game adaptation to repeated play type. The slope across exposures, and they found only pull-up had effect, others small. Not directly about offensive five changes.

None of these directly test "changing the offensive five moves shot mix". So historical_evidence would list these as they are, but they are not directly answering the same question. The prior_work.already_answered is likely "no" or "unknown". However, the records might provide evidence about methodological challenges. For example, SF34 shows that shot mix changes when opponent lineup changes are small and noisy, so power might be limited. SF-TMP-009 shows lineup confounding can create artifacts. SF38 shows that exposure effects are small, and lineup changes might be confounded with game state.

So we need to assess testability. The data: per-game play-by-play with action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result; substitution rotation intervals; starters; defensive matchup minutes; box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database. So we have detailed shot data and substitution timestamps, which could be used to define lineup changes. The question: does changing the offensive five (substitutions) cause a shift in shot mix? That could be examined by comparing the shot mix of possessions immediately before and after a substitution, controlling for score, period, etc. However, there's a risk of confounding because substitutions are not random; they occur due to fouls, fatigue, game situation, etc. So the effect of the lineup change on shot mix could be contaminated by those confounders. That's a key methodological risk: CONFOUNDING. Also, small sample of lineup changes where we have clean before/after windows with enough possessions might lead to SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER. The shot mix shift might be small relative to noise, making it hard to detect. There's also the possibility that if we just look at all substitutions, we might get a spurious effect due to regression to the mean if we select substitutions triggered by unusual shot mix. However, the question is simply "changing the offensive five moves shot mix", not necessarily a causal claim about the lineup causing the shift; but presumably they want to detect a true effect, so confounding could bias. So we must list risks.

The design: estimand could be the difference in shot type distribution (e.g., proportion of three-point attempts, shots at rim, mid-range) in possessions after an offensive substitution compared to before, within the same stint (i.e., before the next substitution), controlling for game context. Unit: a substitution event or a lineup-change window. Sample: all substitutions in the available seasons (three seasons 2022-25). Power: might be enough if they have many substitutions and many possessions, but we need to consider the effect size. SF34 found rim share +0.123 with SE 0.295 when opponent big is off, which is not significant. That's for defense, but offensive changes might have similarly small effects. So sample size could be an issue. However, with three full seasons of data, N substitutions could be thousands, and possessions tens of thousands. So maybe power is adequate for small effects.

But the risk of leakage/lookahead? Not directly.

The question says "showing the design can detect personnel effects." That might be a sanity check: if the design cannot detect the obvious change when you swap a player, then it's not sensitive. So the aim is to demonstrate that the design picks up a signal. That is a methodological validity test. So we should design a test: take all substitutions where the offensive five changes (i.e., a player enters and another exits, excluding timeouts? Or any lineup change). Measure shot mix in the next N possessions (say 5) and compare to the previous N possessions. But need to avoid overlapping possessions: if multiple substitutions close together, need to define windows. Use a difference-in-differences or just before-after? Use a regression with fixed effects for team/season, controlling for score difference, period, etc. Also consider using only "plausibly exogenous" substitutions, such as those due to mandatory stoppages (TV timeouts, quarter breaks) to reduce confounding. However, the statement says "Changing the offensive five itself moves shot mix", which might imply any change, including intentional coaching decisions. So we can't restrict only to exogenous ones, because then the change is still planned. But confounding is present. The design could use an instrumental variable? No.

Maybe the question is simpler: the design can detect personnel effects because when you change the offensive five, the shot mix changes, which indicates that the analytical approach (e.g., using lineup variation) can detect such effects. This could be tested with a simple before-after comparison, but we must consider that shot mix might change due to other reasons. But if we see a significant shift after lineup changes versus control periods (e.g., periods without lineup changes but similar game state), that could demonstrate sensitivity. But then we'd need a control condition. I'll interpret it as a testable claim with proper adjustments.

I'll assign p_testable maybe 0.7, with blocking constraints: confounding (CONFOUNDING) and sample size/power (SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER) if effect small. Also measurement reliability: shot type classification from play-by-play should be reliable. And BASE_RATE? Not needed.

We must structure output. historical_evidence: list the four families, with their status as recorded: FAM:SF34: inconclusive, finding: offenses attack rim more when opponent has no big, but rim share +0.123 SE 0.295, PPP +0.008, inconclusive. FAM:SF-TMP-009: artifact, finding: PULL_UP-specific decline with exposure is defensive adaptation artifact due to lineup confounding. FAM:SF-APPS-076: rejected (null? status as recorded is "rejected", but I see: "auto_outcome_status: rejected" and "observed_verdict: null", so status as recorded is "rejected"? The document says auto_outcome_status: rejected. So we'll use that. Finding: lineup, process, context explain 1.7% of variance, RTM explains 32.9%. FAM:SF38: inconclusive, finding: within-game exposure slope -0.0019 PPP/exposure (SE 0.0019), only pull-up significant.

failed_approaches: from these, which approaches failed? FAM:SF-TMP-009: failure mechanism C_artifact (lineup confounding). So we note that: what_failed: "Using within-game exposure without lineup fixed effects leads to confounding artifact" or something. FAM:SF38: limited by insufficient exposure, low measurement reliability. But FAM:SF38 not a clear failure. FAM:SF-APPS-076: powered null (lineup added zero variance). That could be considered a failed approach to find lineup effects on PPP collapse, indicating lineup variation might not explain that outcome. Could be relevant. But I'd list FAM:SF-TMP-009 as a failed approach due to confounding artifact; others might be limitations.

Then evidence_establishes: from retrieval, it establishes that lineup variation (specifically opponent lineup) can affect shot mix but effects are small and noisy (SF34). It establishes that lineup confounding can produce artifacts in exposure-effect studies (SF-TMP-009). It establishes that lineup effects on PPP collapse are negligible (SF-APPS-076). It establishes that within-game adaptation effects are tiny except for pull-ups (SF38). So overall, the evidence suggests that detecting unambiguous shot mix shifts due to offensive five changes may be challenging because effects might be small and confounded.

evidence_does_not_establish: It does not establish whether changing the offensive five itself causes a detectable shift in shot mix, because no study directly tested that.

own_inferences: based on data available (play-by-play, substitution intervals, shot types), it is feasible to construct a before-after comparison of shot mix around offensive substitutions. However, the main risk is confounding: substitutions often occur due to foul trouble, fatigue, or strategic adjustments, which could also affect shot selection. The effect size might be small relative to game-state variation, leading to low power. Historical findings show that similar lineup-oriented effects (opponent big off floor) yielded imprecise estimates. So while testable, a naive analysis could yield spurious or null results. Proper control for game context (score, period, team fixed effects, shooter fixed effects) and use of a regression discontinuity approach around substitution times could mitigate confounding partially, but residual confounding may remain. Additionally, multiple testing across many shot type categories could inflate false positives.

p_testable: I'll give 0.6, given the power issue and confounding. Blocking constraint: CONFOUNDING (risk of spurious effects due to non-random substitutions), SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER (if the true effect is small, even large sample may be insufficient to reject null). Also measurement reliability: shot type classification (play type) might be noisy, but from play-by-play we have shot distance and action types, so it's reliable enough.

prior_work.already_answered: unknown (no exact match). cited: FAM:SF34, FAM:SF-TMP-009 (these provide relevant context).

risks: list CONFOUNDING, SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER, maybe MEASURE_RELIABILITY (play-type classification?), and RTM_SELECTION (if selecting substitutions based on recent shot mix), but we can define a window that doesn't condition on prior shot mix. Also LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD? No. I'll include risk codes explicitly.

predicted_outcome: I'd weight toward uncertain (inconclusive) or rejected? Given historical noise, maybe uncertain 0.4, supported 0.2, rejected 0.2, artifact 0.1, untestable 0.1. But we need probabilities. I'll do: supported 0.2, rejected 0.3, untestable 0.1, artifact 0.1, uncertain 0.3. Since the question is a methodological claim: "changing the offensive five moves shot mix, showing the design can detect personnel effects." If they test for any shift, they might find a small but significant effect if they have enough power, but confounding could produce an effect. I'll lean uncertain.

Decision: proceed_with_changes: to address confounding, use exogenous substitutions (substitutions at quarter breaks, or due to foul trouble after a foul, but that still might be endogenous). Better: restrict to substitutions that occur after a dead ball (timeout, end of quarter) where the substitution is not a direct response to the preceding play. But still, coaches substitute for reasons correlated with game state. An alternative design: use a difference-in-differences comparing offensive lineup changes that happen due to injury or foul trouble (forced) vs. voluntary ones? Might be complicated. Another approach: use a panel fixed effects for player combinations, but the question is about the act of changing the five. So I'll recommend proceeding with a careful quasi-experimental design: define substitution windows based on the NBA's official substitution times from play-by-play, exclude substitutions that occur within 24 seconds of a strategic timeout? Not sure. I'll design: use all substitutions where the offensive lineup changes (at least one player substitution during a stoppage), compare shot mix in the next N possessions (N=5) versus the preceding N possessions, using a regression with fixed effects for team, season, score difference, period, and also include a control group of "pseudo-substitution" moments when no substitution occurred but similar game clock and score. That could help. But control group construction is tricky. I'll mention a falsification test: test whether shot mix changes at times when no substitution occurred but the same game context (e.g., at random possession boundaries within a quarter) to see if there is a placebo effect. If the effect is only present at real substitutions, that strengthens the case. However, if shot mix naturally varies, we need to adjust.

But the decision is proceed_with_changes: strengthen design to handle confounding, include placebo tests, use appropriate power calculations, pre-register shot mix categories.

I'll output accordingly. The historical effect: the evidence from SF34 suggests that shot mix changes due to opponent lineup changes are imprecise; this may indicate that offensive five effects could also be small, so we need large sample and careful design. The evidence from SF-TMP-009 warns about lineup confounding, which supports inclusion of shooter fixed effects. So evidence changed the decision: originally might have been a simple before-after, but now we incorporate controls and placebo. So changed_decision: yes, explanation: historical evidence from SF34 and SF-TMP-009 highlighted confounding and power concerns, leading to a more robust design with placebo falsification and controls.

Now produce final JSON.
